group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 59-year-old man arrived this afternoon to the peri-operative medicine suite at the request of the vascular surgery team four days before a planned elective open repair of a 5.8-cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm that has grown 7 mm over the past year on serial surveillance CT, prompting the decision to proceed to definitive operative management through a generous midline transperitoneal incision with proximal aortic cross-clamp and direct graft interposition; the surgeons expect the case to last three to four hours with an estimated blood loss of 500–800 mL and plan postoperative admission to the intensive care unit for hemodynamic monitoring, ventilatory weaning, and early extubation if parameters permit. The patient walked from the parking garage carrying a backpack, took the elevator to the clinic, and spoke in full sentences without pausing, stating that he can mow his small lawn with a self-propelled mower and climb two flights of stairs at home while holding a conversation, though he avoids running or shoveling snow because of intermittent pressure across the mid-sternum that predictably arises after brisk exertion and resolves within five minutes of rest; similar exertional discomfort five years ago led to a treadmill nuclear study that demonstrated a reversible inferolateral perfusion defect, and subsequent coronary angiography revealed a 90 % proximal left circumflex lesion successfully treated with a drug-eluting stent. He completed the recommended twelve-month course of dual antiplatelet therapy and now remains on daily aspirin 81 mg and rosuvastatin 40 mg; he has not experienced rest pain, acute coronary syndrome, or hospitalization for cardiac causes since that intervention, and a cardiology review three months ago documented preserved left ventricular systolic function without regional wall-motion abnormalities. Hyperlipidemia and primary hypertension are long-standing and controlled with the statin noted above, lisinopril 20 mg each morning, and amlodipine 5 mg nightly, with home pressures typically in the 120s/70s. Type 2 diabetes was diagnosed twelve years ago; after progressive fasting hyperglycemia despite maximal metformin and lifestyle measures, basal-bolus insulin was introduced two years ago. He currently administers insulin glargine 32 units subcutaneously at bedtime and uses insulin aspart before meals following a 1:12 carbohydrate ratio with a correction factor of one unit for every 30 mg/dL above 140 mg/dL, checking capillary glucose four times daily; a download reviewed by his endocrinologist last month showed 70 % time in the 80–180 mg/dL range, and hemoglobin A1c at that visit was 7.2 %. He denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, ankle swelling, unexplained weight gain, or prior episodes of pulmonary edema; he sleeps flat on one pillow and walks the dog a half mile each evening without dyspnea. No history of stroke, transient ischemic attack, carotid surgery, peripheral arterial bypass, or limb claudication is reported. Surgical history is limited to an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy at age 48 and colonoscopic polypectomy under sedation last year. He smoked one pack per day from age 20 to 45 and quit fourteen years ago; alcohol intake is limited to a bottle of beer with weekend dinner, and he denies recreational drug use. Family history includes a father who underwent coronary artery bypass at 62 and a mother with type 2 diabetes; no early cerebrovascular events or aneurysmal disease are known. Review of systems today is negative for palpitations, presyncope, fever, productive cough, abdominal pain beyond dull midline fullness associated with the aneurysm, gastrointestinal bleeding, leg edema, or urinary complaints. After five minutes of seated rest, vital signs recorded blood pressure 124/70 mm Hg in the right arm, regular pulse 68 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air, oral temperature 36.6 °C, and body mass index 28 kg/m². He appeared comfortable and euvolemic. Neck examination revealed flat jugular venous contours with the head of bed at 45°, carotid upstrokes were brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse was localized in the fifth intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line. Cardiac auscultation disclosed crisp S1 and S2 without gallop, click, or significant murmur; no peripheral stigmata of endocarditis were present. Lungs were clear to percussion and auscultation throughout, and there was no accessory muscle use. The abdomen was soft, nondistended, and demonstrated a palpable pulsatile mass just left of midline without tenderness or bruit; femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses were 2+ and symmetric, and there was no lower-extremity edema or skin discoloration. Neurologic screening revealed full orientation, intact cranial nerves, symmetric 5/5 motor strength, normal light-touch sensation, and a steady tandem gait. Skin inspection showed well-healed laparoscopy scars, and the airway assessment documented Mallampati class II with an inter-incisor distance of 4.2 cm and full neck extension. Pre-operative laboratory studies drawn one hour before examination revealed hemoglobin 14.0 g/dL, hematocrit 42 %, white blood cell count 7.1 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 238 × 10⁹/L, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 22 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.42 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 56 mL/min/1.73 m²; fasting plasma glucose obtained simultaneously measured 128 mg/dL, and liver chemistries and international normalized ratio were within reference limits. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram performed in clinic displayed normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats/min, prior inferolateral Q waves consistent with his known disease, no acute ST-segment or T-wave changes, and unchanged intervals compared with a tracing three months ago. Upright posterior-anterior chest radiography showed clear lung fields, normal cardiomediastinal silhouette, and no evidence of pulmonary vascular congestion or pleural effusion. The anesthesia plan includes general endotracheal anesthesia with intraoperative transesophageal echocardiographic monitoring, arterial line placement for beat-to-beat pressure assessment, continuation of beta-blocking therapy through the morning of surgery, holding the angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor on the day of operation, administering 80 % of the usual basal insulin dose the night before, and hourly point-of-care glucose checks with intravenous dextrose or titrated rapid-acting insulin as indicated. The vascular team counseled the patient on risks of myocardial ischemia, renal impairment, lower-extremity ischemia, graft infection, and respiratory complications, emphasized smoking avoidance, incentive spirometry, and early ambulation, and verified that the patient has arranged postoperative assistance at home; after questions were addressed, he voiced clear understanding and readiness to proceed.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) assigns 1 point for each of six preoperative criteria:
- High-risk surgery: open transperitoneal abdominal aortic aneurysm repair is a suprainguinal vascular operation, +1.
- Ischemic heart disease: exertional angina with known obstructive coronary disease and prior stenting, +1.
- History of heart failure: none documented, 0.
- History of cerebrovascular disease: no prior stroke or TIA, 0.
- Preoperative insulin treatment: uses basal glargine and mealtime aspart, +1.
- Serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: measured 1.42 mg/dL, 0. Reduced eGFR alone does not meet this criterion.
Total = 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 0 = 3.
Final answer: 3
